catalog_quote: [Wilson 1986:287] All of the Wakashan languages distinguish between light and heavy syllables, that is, between non-branching and branching rimes. In Kwakiutlan, a light syllable contains a reduced vowel. The basic stress rule of Kwakwala places primary stress on the first heavy syllable in a word. Secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables after the primary stress. sweep_summary: search for kwak1269 (Kwak'wala, catalog classification weight, deciding source Wilson 1986 BLS 12:287-288) had a single title item: Bach 1975, 'Long vowels and stress in Kwakiutl', Texas Linguistic Forum 2:9-19, already in our bibliography. It is unambiguously about word stress in this language (Glottolog record 671236; Bach's own publication list and Northern Wakashan checklist, the Internet Archive copies saved). No open copy could be found: no DOI/record on Crossref, Semantic Scholar or OpenAlex; archive.org has other TLF volumes but not 1975; the the Internet Archive index of both of Bach's UMass sites shows only three unrelated PDFs; Google Books lists the 1975 TLF volume (id rPZhaRgAEusC, 186 pp.) with no view; HathiTrust, Google Books pages and WorldCat are bot-walled by automated download; Access = print only, priority high (it is the classic first-hand rule statement and the source every later description cites). Its rule is, however, quoted verbatim in the held Janzen 2015 thesis (p.44, scanned verified in this search of works with stress in the title): 'Stress first syllable with long vowel or vowel plus tautosyllabic resonant or if none stress last syllable', and Gordon 2000 and Werle 2010 (both held) transmit the same leftmost-heavy-else-final rule from Bach 1975; so as far as it can be read second-hand it confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and does not supersede Wilson 1986. Nothing new was read first-hand, so no new stress statement was found; three bibliographic pages were and logged in there.

new_statements.quote: As noted above, the stress pattern of Kʷak̓ʷala is described in the literature as default-to-right (Wilson 1978, Wilson 1986, Shaw 2009). [...] Guc̓a follows this pattern of lexical stress. [...] Any syllable with a full vowel nucleus, or with a schwa followed by a plain resonant in coda position, will attract stress, and the first such syllable from the left edge of a word will bear primary stress. If there are only light syllables in a word, the rightmost syllable is stressed. Light syllables are those with a schwa nucleus, such as open syllables with schwa, or schwa followed by a coda obstruent (ə, əO).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kwak'wala (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule; this work supplies it: leftmost heavy (full V or əR), else final. Note the citation is wrong: this is a UC Santa Barbara PhD dissertation (committee Genetti, Gordon, Mithun, Shaw; eScholarship item 2j88d8vb; 158 pp.), not a UBC MA thesis. Describes the Guc̓a (Quatsino) dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable of the word; heavy = full (non-schwa) vowel nucleus, or schwa plus a plain (non-glottalized) resonant coda; if no syllable is heavy, the final syllable is stressed ('default-to-right'). Acoustic correlates: longer duration, higher intensity/F0 on the stressed syllable (sec. 3.4.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Guc̓a (no statement on secondary stress in the thesis).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 68: 'a full vowel followed by a glottal stop (Vʔ) does not attract stress and, second, neither does a schwa followed by a glottalized resonant (əR')' — glottalization makes the syllable light; n. 18: word-final schwa is banned (would-be schwas are /a/), so some 'default' cases look like final full vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Siemens 2016 describes the Guc̓a (Quatsino) dialect of Kwak'wala (Wallas family recordings, 2011-2014) and reports the same pattern as the general Kwak'wala literature (Wilson 1978 on Quatsino; Shaw 2009). Hall 1889 is the Alert Bay missionary grammar of 'Kwagiutl'. The catalog citation for Siemens is wrong: it is a UC Santa Barbara PhD dissertation (eScholarship 2j88d8vb, 158 pp.), not a UBC MA thesis.

new_statements.quote: In sum, Kwak’wala stress system can be restated as follows. Stress falls on the leftmost moraic syllable or the rightmost syllable if there is no moraic syllable in the word. ‘Moraic syllable’ refers to a syllable with a non-schwa nucleus or a plain sonorant coda. In the latter case, the nucleus is usually a non-moraic schwa. (p. 325) [On Zec 1988/1995, p. 323:] According to her analysis, primary stress falls on the leftmost syllable containing a long vowel or the rightmost syllable if there is no syllable containing a long vowel in the word. Despite its popularity, it has been pointed out that Zec’s analysis crucially relies on the controversial assumption that vowel length is contrastive in Kwak’wala (Bach et al. 2005).

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty; agrees with Siemens 2016 on leftmost heavy else final and adds the moraic definition, acoustic correlates and the secondary-stress uncertainty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the leftmost moraic (heavy) syllable — a syllable with a non-schwa nucleus or a plain (non-glottalized) sonorant coda — otherwise on the final syllable. Stressed vowels are longer and have higher F0 (p. 327); stressed syllable carries an H*+L pitch accent in each phonological phrase (p. 337).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 328: 'the existent descriptions of secondary stress are inconsistent and unclear (Boas 1947; Grubb 1969, 1977)'; footing disputed (iambic: Kirchner, Struijke, P. Wilson, Zec; trochaic: Kalmar, S. Wilson); plural-reduplication data (bí-bəgʷànəm vs bi-bábagʷəm) taken to support trochaic feet; p. 329: 'For now, I ignore the issue of footing and secondary stress.'
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa + glottalized sonorant is unstressable (Zec); vowel length treated as non-contrastive, so the 'long vowel' version of the rule (Zec, Bach) is restated in terms of full vowels / sonorant codas. Deictic clitics can take stress when the host loses stressability (p. 331).
new_statements.identity_note: Siemens 2016 describes the Guc̓a (Quatsino) dialect of Kwak'wala (Wallas family recordings, 2011-2014) and reports the same pattern as the general Kwak'wala literature (Wilson 1978 on Quatsino; Shaw 2009). Hall 1889 is the Alert Bay missionary grammar of 'Kwagiutl'. The catalog citation for Siemens is wrong: it is a UC Santa Barbara PhD dissertation (eScholarship 2j88d8vb, 158 pp.), not a UBC MA thesis.

new_statements.quote: Kwakw’ala (Boas 1947; Bach 1975; Wilson 1986) is typically described as a language with a default-to-right stress system, in which the leftmost heavy syllable (=CVV, CVR [R=sonorant]) attracts stress, otherwise the final syllable, as in (2). (p. 101) [...] Boas reports that stems with initial CV, CVO have accent on second or a later syllable (Boas, pg. 218). This leaves open the possibility that words with more than two syllables may have stress on the second syllable, which would be non-final. Such a stress pattern, which actually occurs frequently in Boas’ data, contradicts the default-to-opposite pattern. [...] Without this information, it is difficult to speak confidently of Kwakw’ala as a language with default-to-opposite stress. (p. 109)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reports the standard description (from Bach 1975 / Boas 1947): stress on the leftmost heavy syllable (CVV or CVR), otherwise the final syllable; then argues the 'otherwise final' half rests only on Boas's CəCəCə stems in terminal position, while Boas's data also show second-syllable (non-final) stress in CV/CVO-initial stems, so the default-to-opposite classification is inconclusive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described for Kwak'wala; Gordon notes many default-to-opposite systems turn out to have secondary stress on non-primary heavy syllables, but for Kwak'wala the description is 'inconclusive in certain crucial respects' (p. 108).
new_statements.exceptions: Final-syllable default documented only for CəCəCə stems in terminal (phrase-final) position; words with CV/CVO initial syllables may stress the second syllable (Boas p. 218).
new_statements.identity_note: Siemens 2016 describes the Guc̓a (Quatsino) dialect of Kwak'wala (Wallas family recordings, 2011-2014) and reports the same pattern as the general Kwak'wala literature (Wilson 1978 on Quatsino; Shaw 2009). Hall 1889 is the Alert Bay missionary grammar of 'Kwagiutl'. The catalog citation for Siemens is wrong: it is a UC Santa Barbara PhD dissertation (eScholarship 2j88d8vb, 158 pp.), not a UBC MA thesis.

readall_conflicts: The three substantive sources agree on the placement: primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable, otherwise the final syllable ('default-to-right'). They differ on (a) what counts as heavy — Zec/Bach as reported by Noguchi and Gordon use long vowels (CVV) and CVR, while Noguchi 2011 and Siemens 2016 (with Shaw 2009) say vowel length is not contrastive and define heavy as a full (non-schwa) vowel or schwa + plain resonant coda, with Vʔ and əR' light; (b) the default case — Gordon 2000 argues Boas's data show second-syllable (non-final) stress in CV/CVO-initial stems and that final stress is attested only for CəCəCə stems in terminal position, so he finds the default-to-opposite classification inconclusive, whereas Siemens (citing Shaw 2009) and Noguchi reaffirm final stress in all-light words; (c) footing/secondary stress — descriptions are inconsistent (Boas, Grubb), iambic (Zec, Kirchner, Struijke) vs. trochaic (Kalmar, S. Wilson, Noguchi's reduplication data), unresolved. Hall 1889 is silent; Bach 1975 and Littell 2016 could not be opened.
